To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a discrete event simulation (des) model was developed to predict the long-term health outcomes and costs of smoking and smoking cessation interventions, and (2) the simulation was able to accurately predict outcomes in five randomized clinical trials, and (3) the simulation was also able to predict differences between single and multiple quit attempt simulations.

the DES framework provides a more realistic model of smoking cessation and its outcomes than models that assume a single quit attempt, and can provide more reliable and comprehensive predictions on the long-term health impact of interventions that increase abstinence from tobacco use.

the simulation predicts that allowing for multiple quit attempt strategies results in longer time periods in which smokers are abstinent and lower smoking-related disease costs, and that the simulation can provide estimates of health and economic impacts of interventions designed to promote smoking cessation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a simulation model to evaluate the potential health and economic impact (costs and benefits) of different smoking cessation strategies.
the development and evaluation of a new simulation framework to assess the potential health and economic impact over a lifetime of different strategies to assist smokers to quit.
the development of an individual-based model of smoking cessation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this model can provide a useful framework for evaluating the potential health and economic impact on smokers of various smoking cessation interventions.
the simulation provides an appropriate framework for evaluating the potential health and economic impact on smoking cessation interventions.
DES provides a framework to simulate smoking cessation interventions and outcomes over a lifetime.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a DES model can be used to predict the long-term health impact of smoking cessation interventions and to evaluate the impact of interventions in subgroups of smokers.
the DES model is an appropriate and effective tool for evaluating the health and economic impacts of smoking cessation strategies.
the DES model is a valuable framework for evaluating the health and economic outcomes of smoking cessation treatments and policies.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the health and economic outcomes associated with smoking cessation interventions depend on the number of quit attempts allowed in the simulation, with multiple quit attempts resulting in better long-term outcomes.
the impact of a cessation intervention is best assessed by considering all quit attempts over the smoker’s lifetime, rather than only the first quit attempt.
the impact of smoking cessation interventions on health and economic costs is highly dependent on the underlying assumptions regarding the number of quit attempts and the time between them.
